articles.title: Three powers, one table and the future of global governance
articles.summary: The first trilateral meeting between the leaders of China , Russia and the US was held in Shenzhen. The symbolic value of China's desire to set the table and shape the agenda is greater than the immediate substantive achievements. Its impact will depend on the dynamics between the three countries, as well as the reactions of other powers amid geopolitical fragmentation. Chinese president Xi Jinping called for “maintaining world peace and promoting strategic stability in major power relations” at a meeting of the three largest nuclear powers and permanent members of the UN Security Council. The leaders - Xi Jinping, Russian president Vladimir Putin and US president Donald Trump - discussed a limited agenda and issued a short “Declaration for Peace”. It identified four areas of understanding: reform of the UN to enable an effective response to global challenges; energy security through increased supplies of refined petroleum and stable energy flows; nuclear restraint, dialogue on nuclear risks and preventing proliferation; and limiting the legal jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court. It reflected intent but lacked substance or a diplomatic breakthrough. Donald Trump and Xi Jinping should press Vladimir Putin to end war, not appease him, Ukraine says Shenzhen is not Yalta China’s Global Security Initiative (2022) had prioritised major power diplomacy as a stabilising factor. In contrast, the US National Security Strategy considered China a near-peer economic, technological and Indo-Pacific competitor (2025). Earlier, it had called China the most consequential geopolitical challenge and Russia an acute threat (2022), and described China and Russia as revisionist powers (2017). Relations between China, Russia and the US remain adversarial. The parallels between Shenzhen and Yalta are weak. At Yalta, the victorious allies restructured the global order after the enemy had been defeated; in Shenzhen, the conflicts are ongoing. Shenzhen's focus was on managing competition between powerful adversarial states in a world increasingly characterised by the rise of emerging powers and multi-alignment. Rationale for trilateral meet Domestic compulsions and strategic accommodation between the parties, rather than restructuring of the global system, provide a better understanding of the Shenzhen agenda and objectives. The three leaders had different motivations but a common interest in preventing their strategic competition from escalating into an uncontrollable confrontation. Xi is arguably the biggest immediate beneficiary. He has placed China at the centre of a new diplomatic initiative, presenting it as a stabilising power in global affairs rather than merely as a challenger to US leadership. The summit avoids commitments that could constrain China's strategic relationship with Russia, its freedom of action in the Indo-Pacific or its expansion of regional influence. This flexibility will be helpful ahead of the crucial CCP plenum in 2027. China is a formidable economic and technological powerhouse but faces declining growth, external de-risking and domestic struggles. Its relations with the US have been marked by uncertainty over tariffs, technology and Taiwan. A strategic reset at the major power level was necessary. For Russia, the meeting marks a restoration of great power status. Despite the continuing war in Ukraine and sanctions, Putin’s participation reinforces claims that Russia is an indispensable power. Putin also benefits from direct discussions on Ukraine with the US and China, without Ukraine or Europeans participating in the conversation. For the US, which remains militarily pre-eminent but faces challenges in sustaining global commitments, the trilateral summit gave Trump space for personal diplomacy. The US demonstrated that it could engage simultaneously with two principal strategic competitors, negotiate energy security for domestic benefit and bring China into discussions on nuclear risk and stability. However, Trump's recognition of Putin and Xi as equal interlocutors prompted Europeans to convene their own summit in Berlin to demonstrate support for Ukraine. Future of global governance It is interesting that the three major powers asserted a special responsibility for global affairs, even as it has become evident that India, Japan, Brazil, Europe and others are consequential powers and not passive spectators. It is also ironic that UN reform was addressed in an exclusive format through selective cooperation. There could be attempts at selective multilateralism by the three powers on nuclear security, energy and other issues while they compete in technology, trade and regional geopolitics. There could also be further weakening of multilateral institutions if the accommodation of major power interests takes precedence over the democratisation of decision-making. BRICS 2026 | India must be wary of China’s and Russia’s push for ‘global governance’ India factor For India, the Shenzhen trilateral presents a complex strategic situation. It is simultaneously a challenge, an opportunity and a reminder that the world may be moving towards a more explicit hierarchy of power. First, India would benefit from a significant expansion of hard power and an active presence in global affairs, making it difficult to ignore the country in any emerging architecture of global governance. Second, India's strategic autonomy is more relevant today than ever. India’s strategic partnerships with all three countries, albeit of different types, could convey that any major power accommodation that disregards India's core concerns would be unacceptable. Third, the China question becomes more complicated if Beijing advances a concept of Asian security and global governance without adequately considering India. The Quad, G20, BRICS and SCO acquire significance in this context. Fourth, India must strengthen its Global South leadership, press for reform of the UN Security Council and be at the centre of shaping the rules of an emerging global order. There is fascinating continuity and signalling between the Manila Quad summit and the Shenzhen trilateral summit. For India, the question is no longer whether it will emerge as a major power, but whether it will be an indispensable partner in structures of global governance. For now, India must resist both the temptation of joining an exclusive major power arrangement and the danger of being left outside it. (The writer is a former diplomat and currently Professor at the Jindal Global University) (Disclaimer: The views expressed above are the author's own. They do not necessarily reflect the views of DH.)
